thread.title: Yes, even some Christmas cards send the wrong message and are bad for your health

author: mediabest
title: Yes, even some Christmas cards send the wrong message and are bad for your health
text:
access_time 3 mins ago
Christmas cards featuring alcohol “reflect and reinforce a social attitude that excess alcohol consumption is acceptable and associated with celebration,” according to a warning issued in an article in the latest issue of the British Medical Journal.
Tracey Polak, assistant director of public health, and Virginia Pearson, chief officer for communities, public health, environment and prosperity at Devon County Council, said Christmas and birthday cards “influence views on drinking and reinforce this as a social norm.”
They cited cards with phrases like “let’s get wrecked,” “all the gin” and “trollied” printed across images of people who are “clearly” inebriated on some greeting cards, “surrounded by empty bottles, drinking directly from a bottle, or in some case unconscious.”
Of course, many Christmas cards don’t feature Santa Claus swinging a tankard of beer, and many birthday cards don’t show off-color jokes about drinking alcohol. There are approximately 6.5 billion greeting cards sold each year, according to industry estimates.
Sir Henry Cole is credited with popularizing the first Christmas card in the U.K. in 1843, depicting a scene showing people drinking, the authors added. A 1980 analysis of greeting cards revealed themes that suggested that drinking is a desirable and harmless part of celebrations, they noted.
The writers in the British Medical Journal also added that the responsibility for choosing cards lies with the purchaser “so perhaps it is worth reflecting the next time that you choose one whether the message is one that you condone and wish to pass on.”
The Washington, D.C.-based Greeting Card Association says the most popular seasonal cards are Christmas cards, with approximately 1.6 billion units purchased (including boxed cards). The association says Facebook FB, +1.00% messages has had only a minor impact on the industry.
“The tradition of giving greeting cards as a meaningful expression of personal affection for another person is still being deeply ingrained in today’s youth,” the association said in a statement on its website, adding that young Americans also send cards online.
The association was not immediately available for comment.

Indeed, any amount of alcohol is dangerous to consume, a study published earlier this year in the international medical journal The Lancet found. The report examined 694 data sources and 592 prospective and retrospective studies and said alcohol is a major cause of death globally.
At the time of the report, the Distilled Spirits Council, a trade association, said the study went too far. It said previous research has suggested that drinking alcohol in moderation could have positive health benefits. It added that increasing taxes on alcohol could increase illicit alcohol production.
On the gifts front, analyst firm Piper Jaffray recently said the No. 1 item on U.S. teenagers’ wish list this holiday season is Apple’s AAPL, -2.24% iPhone. In fact, their top four consumer brands — Apple Watch, MacBooks and Airpods — all come in those iconic white boxes with the apple symbol.
These brands were followed by Gucci PPRUY, -1.30% Vans, Adidas ADDYY, +0.58% and Lululemon LULU, -1.14% and NBA 2k19, a basketball simulation video game. Apple accounted for 11.5% of teens’ wish lists. The next closest brand, Gucci, accounted for just 0.6%.
(Kari Paul contributed to this story.)
